This page details the recommended Jet Energy Scale (JES) and Resolution (JER) uncertainty schemes available for use in R22 physics analyses.
Below, many details about specific aspects of the JES and JER uncertainties are provided in order to help users avoid common problems.
 We recommend strongly that everyone performing ATLAS physics analyses with jets reads this page before starting their analysis!
R22 JES Pre-Recommendations
Preliminary jet calibrations and uncertainties are available for EMPFlow jets in R22 data and simulation. Different calibrations are available for Run 2 conditions(2015/16/17/18 data and MC20a/d/e) and Run 3 conditions (2022/23 and MC23a/c) high-µ data (re)processed with R22.
This 'pre-recommendation' consists of a dedicated MC20 (MC23)-based calibration for Run-2 (Run-3) (area subtraction, pileup residual, absolute JES and GlobalSequential Calibration) and applies the R21 in situ calibration to all data reprocessed with R22+. The uncertainties associated with that calibration are provided to the user,in the CategoryReduction and either SimpleJER or FullJER scheme.
 These uncertainties are only supported in Release 22.2.108+
 There are presently no calibrations or uncertainties for LCTopoJets or CSSKUFOJets reconstructed in R22 with any jet radius parameter. For EMTopoJets a dedicated setof recommendations was derived by Long Lived Particles physics analyses team members. The calibration strategy does not include the Global Sequential Calibration stepand the uncertainties were derived following a similar procedure as the one used for R=0.4 particle-flow jet.
JetEtMiss does not currently support MC2MC corrections or per-jet flavour treatment for R22 pre-recommendations, but hopes to include these improvements again in futurecalibrations. If the sensitivity of your analysis is limited by JES/JER/JMS/JMR performance, we encourage analysis teams to study the JetEtmissHighPriorityTasks page and
 contact the JetEtMiss conveners to get involved!
How to correlate Run2 and Run3 pre-recommendations
For pre-recommendations, the NPs are mostly coming from the same in-situ measurement performed with Run2 data, so NPs with the same name should be treated as fullycorrelated. The only exceptions are:InSitu _NonClosure_PreRecEtaIntercalibration _NonClosure_R10_PreRecInSitu _NonClosure_R10_PreRecAF3 components
Only the Category scheme is available for pre-recommendations, so this scheme should be used consistently in the input results. More schemes are foreseen to be availablein the next set of recommendations.
How to correlate small-R and large-R pre-recommendations
The method to correlate small-R and large-R JES/JER is the same as in release 21, documented in this Twiki.

Jet energy scale (JES) uncertainties : background information
Overview
The JES uncertainties come from several primary sources. They are:Relative in situDijet eta-intercalibration: calibrate the scale of forward jets with respect to central jetsDepends on jet pT and eta
More relevant for more forward jetsAbsolute in situZ+jet balance: calibrate the scale of jets with respect to a well understood object (Zee, Zµµ)Ddepends on jet pT
Mostly relevant for low pT (below roughly 100 GeV)
Photon+jet balance: calibrate the scale of jets with respect to a well understood object (photon)Depends on jet pT
Mostly relevant for medium pT (from roughly 100 GeV to 1 TeV)
Multijet balance: calibrate the scale of jets with respect to a well understood object (a recoil system of lower-pT, calibrated jets)
Depends on jet pT
Mostly relevant for high jet pT (from roughly 1 TeV to 2 TeV)
Single-hadron response and test beam uncertaintiesDepends on jet pT
Mostly relevant for extremely high jet pT (above the end of the multi-jet balance, ~2 TeV)
Pileup uncertaintiesDepend on jet pT, jet eta, NPV and mu (exact variables depend on the uncertainty component)
Mostly relevant for low jet pT (below roughly 50 GeV)
Flavour-related uncertaintiesDepend on at least jet pT and jet eta, perhaps more
Depends on whether or not the user identifies b-jetsDepends on whether or not the user specifies their own flavour composition ()Depends on whether or not that flavour composition is specified by jet multiplicity ()Depends on whether or not that jet multiplicity flavour composition is specified by process ()Potentially relevant for low-to-medium jet pT (below several hundred GeV)
Punch-through uncertaintyDepends on jet pT, jet eta, and the number of muon segments behind the jet
Potentially relevant for analyses which are sensitive to muon spectrometer activity close to jetsOtherwise, limited relevant to the high-jet pT regime (above 1 TeV)
MC non-closure uncertaintyDepends on jet pT and jet etaThis term is zero if you are using full simulationThis term is non-zero if you are using fast simulation (AtlasFast3)
-->
Jet energy resolution (JER) uncertainties : background information
Overview
The JER uncertainties come from a few primary sources. They are:Data vs MC differenceDepends on pT and etaDerived to account for differences between the nominal MC and data JERIf MC is better than data, we smear the MC to match dataIf data is better than MC, we don't want to degrade the data to match a given MCThis uncertainty is only non-zero when the nominal data resolution is superior to the nominal MC resolutionThis uncertainty differs depending on if you have configured the tool using MC20 or MC21 (fullsim) or AFII (fastsim)The resulting uncertainty name also differs to reflect this (e.g. JET_JER_DataVsMC_MC20 vs JET_JER_DataVsMC_AFII)If you are using both fullsim and fastsim samples, then these two components should be treated separatelyNoise term evaluation from random cones in zero bias dataDepends on pT and etaMostly relevant for low pT (below 100 GeV)In situ dijet pT balance asymmetryDepends on pT and etaRelevant almost everywhere (from a few tens of GeV to the highest pT)

There are three types of smearing configurations, as mentioned earlier. They are named either "AllJERNP", "FullJER", or "SimpleJER". For the first two cases, theuncertainties smear both (pseudo-)data and MC events. In the latter case of the "SimpleJER", only the MC is smeared. The implications are as follows:(Pseudo-)data and MC smearingThis is the most correct thing to do, and should be the default for any analysis where the JER is a non-negligible uncertainty.Shifting a given NP by +1 sigma will correspond with smearing either the (pseudo-)data or MC, while shifting the same NP by -1 sigma will correspond withsmearing the MC or (pseudo-)data.If the uncertainty for a given component crosses zero, then this will change whether (pseudo)-data or MC is smeared, thus properly retaining the anti-correlatedbehaviour implied by the uncertainty, rather than enforcing a correlated behaviour.MC-only smearingThis is an approximation, and is acceptable for analyses where the JER is a negligible uncertainty.Shifting a given NP by +1 sigma or -1 sigma will return the same result, where the MC is smeared in both cases by the same factor. The analysis musttherefore manually symmetrize the uncertainty.If the uncertainty for a given component crosses zero, then this will force a correlated behaviour, thus ignoring the anti-correlation implied by crossing zero. Theanalysis therefore is changing the correlation structure of the JER uncertainties.
To repeat, if the JER is a non-negligible uncertainty, you should use the full (pseudo-)data and MC smearing configurations. The MC-only smearing variant is asimplification for analyses which are not sensitive to the JER.
In some cases, an analysis may be sensitive to the JER, but it may not be possible to smear the data. For example, if the analysis has a very small number of data events,then smearing the data can lead to arbitrarily large fluctuations that have to deal with the statistics of the sample rather than the JER. In such cases, pseudo-data can be usedinstead of data. Examples of pseudo-data techniques and where they are relevant can be found on this twiki.
A detailed description about how to use the fullJER uncertainties can be found in this presenation
 .
⚠  For analyses using the fullJER: pay special attention to slides 7-11 of the presentation above
  where it is explained how to construct the JER systematics in youranalysis from the combination of (pseudo-)data and MC smearing NPs provided by the JetUncertainties tool. To be clear, one should not propagate independently theseNPs but build templates using them.
Using the JetUncertainties tool
Getting the JetUncertainties tool code
The JetUncertainties package and associated tool should already be included in the (Ath)Analysis* release that you are using. In case you are not using such a release,you likely already know how to check it out. The tool lives in the directory Reconstruction/Jet/JetUncertainties ( link
 ).
Configuring and initializing the tool
The tool has four mandatory parameters that you must specify:
JetDefinition, a string
AntiKt4EMPFlow for R=0.4 jets built from particle-flow objects
MCType, a stringMC20 or MC21 for full simulation samples
ConfigFile, a stringThe name of the config file, including the relevant folders. See above for the available config files.
IsData, a booleanYou can skip this if you only use the JES, but this is a new parameter that is strictly necessary for the JERThis flag should be "true" if you are running over data (or pseudo-data) and "false" if you are running over MCThis has zero impact on the JES uncertainties, but controls how the JER uncertainties are applied
The tool has a few optional parameters that are not normally relevant but which may be useful in specific circumstances:
CalibArea, a stringIf the tool default is not pointing to the CalibArea version that you want, you can force the tool to look at a different CalibArea version by setting this flag
Path, a stringIf you want to read config files from an area other than the CalibArea, then this option can be specified, pointing to the directory to read from instead. Note that ifthe tool fails to find the specified files in this directory, it will fall back on CalibArea.
AnalysisFile, a string
If you are specifying the flavour composition for your analysis, this should be the full path to the relevant root file to read the composition histograms from.
Athena example:
ToolSvc += CfgMgr.JetUncertaintiesTool ("JESProv", JetDefinition ="AntiKt4EMPFlow", MCType="MC20", ConfigFile ="rel22/Summer2023_PreRec/R4_CategoryReduction_
Get a ToolHandle to the tool you have created:
#include "JetCPInterfaces/ICPJetUncertaintiesTool.h"
#include "GaudiKernel/ToolHandle.h"
ToolHandle <ICPJetUncertaintiesTool> jesProv("JESprov");
CHECK(jesProv.retrieve());

Tool requirements and assumptions
For the most part, the above instructions should work without problem for users. However, in some cases, additional user-specified data is required. In particular, the
xAOD::Jet and xAOD::EventInfo objects are expected to contain certain variables. Below is a list of these assumptions:
xAOD::Jet variables:
GhostMuonSegmentCount: The number of muon segments associated to the jet. This should be part of the Jet without any user input, so long as the user has notremoved this information from their xAOD file.
IsBjet: Whether the user considers the jet as a b-jet (true) or light quark/gluon jet (false) for the flavour uncertainties. This is expected to be the most commonreason for the user to modify a jet before asking for its uncertainty. If the user does not specify this variable, it is assumed that it is a light quark/gluon jet, as hasbeen done in the past. This is generally conservative for b-jets on the per-jet level, but not necessarily once correlations are considered between the flavour andb-jet terms in events containing both b-tagged and non-b-tagged jets. Profiling may also change this picture. (NOTE: this is to be done using truth-labelling(PartonTruthLabelID moment) plus any analysis-specific kinematic selections used to define b-jets applied to the nominally calibrated kinematic values.)
xAOD::EventInfo variables:
NPV: The number of primary vertices is expected to be specified within this object. Users should not have to worry about this as it is done automatically, so long
as the user does not specify the EventInfo object directly, and so long as the "PrimaryVertices" collection has not been removed from the xAOD file. For non-standard use cases, it is important that this variable is set by the user.
Njet: The number of user-selected good jets in the event. This is only necessary for users who provide their own flavour composition files, and divide thecomposition in bins of jet multiplicity. If the user is performing such an analysis, they need to fill this variable within EventInfo.
An example of how to set the IsBjet moment :
xAOD::Jet* jet = ; // get the jet you want to modify
bool isBjet = ; // decide whether or not the jet is a b-jet (truth-labelling + kinematic selections)
SG::AuxElement::Accessor<char> accIsBjet("IsBjet"); // char due to limitations of ROOT I/O, still treat it as a boolean value
accIsBjet(*jet) = isBjet;
